name: General Python Placement Assessment
description: A 40-question multiple-choice placement test spanning the full Python Apprentice and Python Games concept range. Used to place a prospective student into the right course and starting lesson.

placement_rubric.explanation: Score each band as a percentage of its questions answered correctly. Walk the bands in order; the student is placed at the START of the first band scoring below the mastery threshold. If every band is mastered, use 'placed_beyond'.

placed_beyond.note: Mastered all assessed Python content — ready for Python Games projects or the next level (Java). Recommend instructor review.

questions.question: What is the overall goal of this program?
options: Ask for one number and double it
Ask for two numbers and display their sum
questions.answer: Ask for two numbers and display their sum
questions.explanation: The opening docstring says to ask for two numbers and display the sum.

questions.question: If you collect both numbers as strings and use +, what happens?
questions.explanation: With strings, + concatenates, so you must convert to numbers to add.

questions.question: Which method hides the main window so only the dialogs show?
questions.explanation: The comment hints to use the withdraw method to hide the window.

questions.question: Based on the age groups, which message fits an age of 15?
questions.explanation: 15 falls in the 13-19 range, which is the Teen group.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
a = 5
s = "hello there"
if a == 5 and s.startswith('hello'):
    print("Hooray!")
questions.explanation: a == 5 is True and s starts with 'hello', so both sides of and are True.

questions.question: Which call asks the user for their age as a whole number?
questions.explanation: askinteger() returns the user's answer as an integer.

questions.question: Which operator should go in the blank to check whether a equals 10 inside an if statement?
questions.explanation: Use == to compare for equality; a single = would assign instead.

questions.question: What does print(bin(11)) display?
questions.explanation: bin() returns a string with a 0b prefix, and 11 in binary is 1011.

questions.question: Using the place values, what is the binary number 10110101 in decimal?
questions.explanation: Add the place values with a 1: 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 1 = 181.

questions.question: Given a = 10, what does print(a == 11) display?
questions.explanation: a is 10, not 11, so the comparison evaluates to False.

questions.question: What does this loop print?
questions.explanation: It prints i, and 5 prints before the break fires (the check comes after the print).

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
from itertools import chain
list1 = [1, 2, 3]
list2 = ['a', 'b', 'c']
for item in chain(list1, list2):
    print(item, end=' ')
questions.explanation: chain() yields all of list1 first, then all of list2.

questions.question: What does the continue statement do?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration and goes back to the start of the loop
questions.answer: Skips the rest of the current iteration and goes back to the start of the loop
questions.explanation: continue jumps to the next loop iteration without finishing the current body.

questions.question: What does count() from itertools produce?
options: A list of exactly ten numbers
The count of items in a list
questions.explanation: count() is an infinite iterator returning numbers sequentially.

questions.question: Why must cycle() almost always be combined with islice() or a break?
options: Because cycle() repeats forever and would otherwise never stop
Because cycle() only works on numbers
questions.answer: Because cycle() repeats forever and would otherwise never stop
questions.explanation: cycle() is infinite, so you need something to limit it.

questions.question: When a number is displayed, how is its color decided?
options: Blue if the sum of its digits is even, red if odd
Blue if the number is even, red if odd
questions.answer: Blue if the sum of its digits is even, red if odd
questions.explanation: The lesson colors by the sum of the digits, not the number itself.

questions.question: When does the else block on a loop run?
options: When the loop finishes normally, but not if break ends it
Every time the loop body runs
Only when the loop body never runs
questions.answer: When the loop finishes normally, but not if break ends it
questions.explanation: The else clause runs on normal completion and is skipped by break.

questions.question: What does this loop print on its first iteration?
questions.explanation: Without unpacking, enumerate yields a tuple of the index and item, starting at 0.

questions.question: In the Euler-style version, the value n**4 % 15 is always one of which set?
questions.explanation: The lesson states these are the only remainders, each mapping to a label.

questions.question: According to the rules, which divisibility check must come first?
questions.explanation: Any multiple of 15 is also a multiple of 5 and 3, so check 15 first.

questions.question: What does the program print for i = 10?
questions.explanation: 10 is divisible by 5 but not 15 or 3, so the badger branch runs.

questions.question: Given the array below, what does two_dimensional_array[1][2] return?
questions.explanation: Index [1] is the second row [4,5,6], and [2] picks the third element, 6.

questions.question: How is the Tic Tac Toe board stored?
options: As a 3x3 2D array (a list of lists)
As a single flat list of 9 items
questions.answer: As a 3x3 2D array (a list of lists)
questions.explanation: The board is built as a 3x3 grid where each cell starts as None.

questions.question: Inside update_listbox, which dict method gives you both the word and its definition to build each display string?
questions.explanation: items() yields key-value pairs, which you can turn into strings.

questions.question: What does check_row return when there is no winner on the line it is given?
questions.explanation: The docstring says it returns the token if there is one, otherwise None.

questions.question: How should check_win be built, according to the instructions?
options: By calling check_row for each row, column, and diagonal
By comparing the whole board to a winning board
By counting the number of X marks
questions.answer: By calling check_row for each row, column, and diagonal
questions.explanation: check_win reuses check_row on every line of the board.

questions.question: Given my_dict = {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3}, what does 'a' in my_dict return?
questions.explanation: For a dict, in checks for the existence of a key, and 'a' is a key.

questions.question: Using the functions f(a, b) = a + b and g(c, d) = c + d, what is the value of g(f(1, 2), f(3, 4))?
The instructions say to use which values for the player marks inside your functions?
questions.explanation: The file says to use the constants instead of the raw strings.

questions.question: What does list(set(my_list)) produce when my_list = ['a','a','b','b','c','c']?
options: A list of the unique items: 'a', 'b', 'c'
A set of all six items
questions.answer: A list of the unique items: 'a', 'b', 'c'
questions.explanation: Converting to a set removes duplicates, then back to a list keeps the unique items.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between a class and an object?
options: A class is a copy of an object
A class is a blueprint and an object is built from it
An object is a blueprint for a class
They are exactly the same thing
questions.answer: A class is a blueprint and an object is built from it
questions.explanation: A class defines the type; an object is one instance made from that blueprint.

questions.question: What does the line class Parent(Person): mean?
questions.explanation: Putting Person in the parentheses makes Parent a derived class of Person.

questions.question: When does the __init__ method run?
options: Automatically when a new object is created
Only when you call it by name
questions.answer: Automatically when a new object is created
questions.explanation: __init__ is the initializer that runs as the object is built.

questions.question: What does polymorphism mean?
options: A class can have many objects
The same method name can do different things in different classes
A program can have many classes
questions.answer: The same method name can do different things in different classes
questions.explanation: 'Poly' means many and 'morph' means form, so the method takes many forms.

questions.question: Given the Person class, which line creates a Person object named Alice who is 14?
questions.explanation: Calling the class like a function runs __init__ and builds the object.

questions.question: What will this code print?
questions.explanation: alice.name returns the value stored when the object was created.

questions.question: The function get_name_and_age(person) was written for a Person. Why can you also pass it a Parent or a Child object?
options: Because Parent and Child are kinds of Person (polymorphism)
Because all functions accept any object
Because Parent and Child have no __init__
questions.answer: Because Parent and Child are kinds of Person (polymorphism)
questions.explanation: Derived classes can be used anywhere their base class is expected.

questions.question: Which symbol do you use to access an object's attribute or method, like getting alice's name?
questions.explanation: alice.name uses the dot to reach the name attribute inside the object.
